titel: Buying or renting in the US
kurz: Why a comparison of buying and renting is about the unrecoverable costs of owning and not the mortgage payment, and why it has to include the return that the down payment would have earned elsewhere.

bloecke.md:
The saying “rent is money thrown away” is not wrong, but it is incomplete. Buying also involves money flowing out that does not build wealth: interest to the lender, property tax to the county or city, premiums to the insurer, maintenance to contractors, closing costs when you buy and agent commissions when you sell. Only one part of the monthly mortgage payment, the principal, turns into wealth, and this part does not belong in a cost calculation.

A clean comparison therefore sets the unrecoverable costs of owning against the rent of a comparable home, not the mortgage payment against the rent. Costs that arise in roughly the same amount on both sides are left out, such as electricity, heating and internet. Property tax is different in the US. The owner pays it directly, while a tenant only pays it indirectly through the rent, so it belongs on the buying side. The same applies to homeowners insurance, which costs far more than a renter's policy.

With the principal portion of the payment, money flows from the account into reducing the debt without being used up. It therefore belongs in the balance sheet of your wealth, not in the cost calculation. The cost comparison includes mortgage interest, property tax, homeowners insurance, maintenance, any HOA dues or mortgage insurance, the closing and selling costs spread over the holding period and the return that the cash put into the home would have earned elsewhere.

## Price-to-rent ratio and gross rental yield

The [[Price-to-rent ratio|price-to-rent ratio]] is the purchase price divided by the annual rent of a comparable home. It can be determined as a first indicator even before a viewing and is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A ratio of 15 corresponds to 6.7%, a ratio of 25 to only 4%.

The calculation uses the rent without utilities. The ratio is not yet a valuation of the property, but it does set a limit. It shows the highest ongoing return the home can deliver before property tax, insurance, maintenance and vacancy are deducted. In the US, these costs are higher than in many other countries, mainly because of property tax, so the gap between gross and net yield is wide.

bloecke.formel:
Price-to-rent ratio = Purchase price / Annual rent
Gross rental yield = 100 / Price-to-rent ratio
bloecke.erklaerung: Both indicators contain the same information. The ratio is common in conversation; the yield allows a comparison with mortgage rates and other investments.
variablen: 12 monthly rents of a comparable home, excluding utilities

bloecke.titel: Gross rental yield by price-to-rent ratio
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. From a ratio of 16 upwards the gross rental yield is at or below the 6.25% mortgage rate assumed in this lesson, and that is before property tax, insurance and maintenance. The assumed rate is not a published figure; current averages are in Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey.

bloecke.md:
## Model case: a single-family house

The model case is a single-family house with a purchase price of $400,000 and no homeowners association. The buyer puts down 20%, that is, $80,000, and pays closing costs of $12,000 or 3% of the price. Lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, recording fees and, depending on the state, transfer taxes add up to a range of roughly 2% to 5% in typical purchases. The cash needed at closing is therefore $92,000. The mortgage amounts to $320,000, which is 80% of the price, so no private mortgage insurance is required.

The calculation assumes a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6.25%. Between 2023 and 2025, the weekly average for 30-year fixed loans in Freddie Mac's survey mostly moved between about 6% and just under 8%; the figure here is an assumption, not a forecast. The fully amortizing payment, an [[Annuity|annuity]], is $1,970.30 a month for principal and interest, that is, $23,644 a year. Of this, $19,894 goes on interest and $3,750 on principal in the first year.

The forgone return on the $92,000 is set at 4.0% after tax, about $3,680 a year. Property tax is assumed at 1.0% of the price, $4,000 a year; actual effective rates range from well under 0.5% to above 2% depending on state and locality. Homeowners insurance is set at $2,000 a year and maintenance at 1% of the price, $4,000, a common rule of thumb. When the house is sold, agent commissions and seller closing costs are due; they are set at 6% of today's price, $24,000.

bloecke.titel: Breakdown of housing costs of $3,098 a month
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for the case above. The forgone return and the spread transaction costs, the items most often missing in conversations, together account for $607 a month.

bloecke.md:
In the first year, unrecoverable costs of $37,174 for ownership compare with $26,400 in rent. Ownership therefore costs $10,774 more than renting. That alone is not yet an argument against buying, because the figure only describes the starting point. Two developments in the following years are not yet included in it.

First, the interest portion falls because the balance falls. With a 30-year loan this happens slowly: averaged over ten years, interest comes to around $18,600 instead of $19,894. Part of this saving is offset, because the equity tied up in the house grows with every principal payment, and with it the forgone return, which reaches around $5,400 in the tenth year. Over the ten years, the costs of owning therefore average around $36,700. Second, rents tend to rise while the principal and interest payment of a fixed-rate loan does not. Property tax and insurance can rise, however, and the advantage of buying arises from the difference between these developments, not from the first year.

If the rent rises by 3% a year, it averages around $30,300 over the ten years instead of $26,400. The gap to the costs of owning of around $36,700 thus narrows to about $6,400 a year. Over ten years, this adds up to around $64,200.

For buying to draw level, the house must gain these $64,200 in value within ten years. That is around 16%, or just under 1.5% a year. Selling costs are already included at today's price; with a higher sale price they rise slightly. Whether such an increase is realistic depends on the local market. Nationally, US home prices fell by roughly a quarter between 2006 and 2012 according to the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Index and rose strongly afterwards. An increase of this order of magnitude is therefore achievable, but not certain.

Closing costs do not increase the value of the house, and the commission and other selling costs are due on top when you sell. As soon as the purchase has closed, the closing costs are sunk. A buyer who resells the house the next day at the same price loses the $12,000 in closing costs plus around $24,000 in selling costs.

Two conclusions follow from this. First, these amounts have to be earned back over the holding period, and the shorter the holding period, the more heavily they weigh on each individual year. Second, closing costs that are not paid in cash still have to be paid: a seller credit is usually priced into the purchase price, and a lender credit or a no-closing-cost loan is paid for with a higher interest rate. How high the costs turn out also depends on the state and the local custom. Some states levy no transfer tax at all, while some states and cities charge several, and who pays which item is often a matter of local practice and negotiation.

bloecke.titel: Monthly housing costs by holding period
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for the same house with holding periods of different lengths. If the house is sold after three years, closing and selling costs alone account for $1,000 a month.

bloecke.md:
## Mobility of tenants and owners

A typical residential lease runs for twelve months, and month-to-month tenancies can usually be ended with a notice period that state law sets, often 30 days. An owner can repay the mortgage at any time; since 2014, federal rules have banned prepayment penalties on most residential mortgages and strictly limited them on the rest (12 CFR 1026.43(g)). The mortgage is therefore rarely the obstacle. The obstacle is the sale itself, with marketing time, commission and other selling costs and a market situation that does not follow your own timetable. On top of this, an owner with a low fixed rate gives it up when moving, because most conventional loans cannot be taken along to the next home.

No general rule follows from this, but a condition for buying does. For buyers who expect to change job or city within five years, their own expectation argues against buying. The holding period affects the result of this calculation more than any other variable, more even than half a percentage point on the interest rate.

## Fivefold leverage and cluster risk

After the purchase, $80,000 of the buyer's own money is in the house, because the $12,000 in closing costs has been used up. The house is worth $400,000, which corresponds to leverage of five to one. If the price falls by 10%, $40,000 is lost, that is, half of the down payment. In a portfolio, such a position would be a gross violation of every diversification rule. It would be a single, illiquid and debt-financed investment in a single location, often amounting to a multiple of the remaining wealth. With an owner-occupied home, this concentration is considered normal because it comes with living there. That explains it, but it does not reduce the risk.

When you sell your main home, Section 121 of the Internal Revenue Code excludes up to $250,000 of gain from income, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly, if you owned and lived in the home for at least two of the five years before the sale. Gains above this are taxed as capital gains.

The mortgage interest deduction helps less than its reputation suggests. Interest on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt counts as qualified residence interest, but only if you itemize deductions instead of taking the standard deduction. In the model case, first-year interest and property tax add up to $23,894. For a married couple filing jointly, that is below the 2026 standard deduction of $32,200, so the interest saves no tax unless other itemized deductions, such as state income tax within the SALT cap or charitable gifts, make up the difference. Investments of the renter are also taxed mildly: in a taxable account, gains on index funds are only taxed when sold, and long-term gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%. This is why the forgone return here is set at 4.0% after tax.

schritte.text: Divide the purchase price by the annual rent of a comparable rental home. What counts is the rent asked in current listings for this location and size, not the rent you would like to see.
Take the closing costs from the lender's Loan Estimate and estimate the selling costs at resale. Spread both over the planned holding period.

schritte.titel: Use interest instead of the payment
schritte.text: Include only the interest portion of the first year, roughly the loan amount times the interest rate. Principal is left out.

schritte.titel: Apply a return to the cash
schritte.text: Apply a realistic after-tax return to all the cash put in at closing, including the closing costs. This item decides the calculation more often than people expect.

Look up the actual property tax bill and the tax rate that will apply after the sale, get an insurance quote, add HOA dues and mortgage insurance if any, and budget maintenance at around 1% of the price, more for older houses.
Leave out utilities on both sides. The remaining difference first has to be recouped through an increase in value.

bloecke.titel: Limits of common rules of thumb
bloecke.md:
One rule says that owning costs about 5% of the home's value a year in unrecoverable costs, about 1% each for property tax and maintenance and about 3% as the cost of capital, so buying pays if the annual rent is above 5% of the price. The 3% for the cost of capital only fits a world of low interest rates. In the model case, interest and forgone return alone come to almost 6% of the price, and the true figure is above 9%. A threshold for the ratio is therefore only meaningful together with the interest rate.

Conversely, the rule “the payment is just like rent” does not work either. It leaves out property tax, insurance, maintenance, forgone return and transaction costs, and instead counts principal as a cost. By coincidence, these errors partly cancel each other out and therefore go unnoticed for a long time.

One argument cannot be captured in any calculation. The fully amortizing mortgage enforces saving. Households that, without this compulsion, would spend the difference instead of investing it are better off with ownership after twenty years, even if the calculation shows the opposite. This argument concerns behaviour, not return. It is nevertheless valid, but must not be mistaken for a return.

mitnehmen: The comparison sets the unrecoverable costs of owning (interest, property tax, insurance, maintenance, spread closing and selling costs and the forgone return on the cash put in) against the rent, not the mortgage payment against the rent.
Principal is a reallocation of wealth and does not belong in the cost calculation; property tax, on the other hand, is paid directly only by the owner and belongs on the buying side.
The price-to-rent ratio is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield and can only be classed as high or low in comparison with the current mortgage rate.
Closing costs of around 2% to 5% and selling costs at resale are sunk costs and make short holding periods expensive in arithmetical terms.
In the model case, buying only draws level with renting after ten years if the house gains just under 1.5% in value a year; that is achievable, but not a given.

begriffe.text: The purchase price divided by the annual rent of a comparable home, and therefore the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A ratio of 15 corresponds to 6.7%, a ratio of 25 to 4%.

The annual rent relative to the purchase price, calculated before closing costs and before property tax, insurance, maintenance and vacancy. It serves as a quick indicator and is not a return in the investment sense.
The after-tax return that the down payment and closing costs would have earned elsewhere. If this item is missing from the comparison, the purchase appears cheaper than it is.
Closing costs at purchase and commission and seller costs at sale. They do not increase the value of the home and have to be earned back over the holding period.

Up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for married couples filing jointly, on the sale of a main home is excluded from income if the owner owned and used it as a main home for at least two of the five years before the sale.
